title: Forgetting in the short-term memory: A replication study
abstract: The study aims at investigating whether the loss of information from the short-term memory is caused mainly by decay or by interference. The procedure is an exact replication of the classic study done by Waugh and Norman (1965).

title: Gender Identity Salience and Completing the Gender System Justification Scale: A Replication Study
abstract: Study Overview This study replicates and extends a word-fragment task experiment testing whether completing the Gender System Justification (GSJ) scale heightens the accessibility of gender identity–related concepts, depending on whether participants are also exposed to unrelated distractor measures. Theoretical Background According to the identity-distraction hypothesis, completing surveys with items unrelated to a participant’s social identity (e.g., gender) reduces the salience of that identity for members of disadvantaged groups when responding to system justification measures (e.g., GSJ). However, because the GSJ scale itself contains gender-related terms, it may instead increase gender salience. This identity-trigger hypothesis predicts that completing the GSJ scale accentuates, rather than diminishes, the relevance of gender identity. Original Experiment In an earlier study (N = 605), participants were randomly assigned to complete measures related to gender identity, national identity, or a distraction (watching a video of a car advert that featured only auto-parts but not people), before a word-fragment task. Results supported both hypotheses: (a) In the distraction condition, participants generated more gender-unrelated than gender-related words, consistent with the identity-distraction hypothesis. (b) In the GSJ condition, participants generated more gender-related than gender-unrelated words, consistent with the identity-trigger hypothesis. Meanwhile (c) in the national identity condition, there was no discernible difference in word fragment completions with gender-related vs. gender-unrelated expression. Also, across the three conditions combined, women more often produced gender-related (vs. gender-unrelated) word-fragment completions, while this was absent for men, suggesting greater salience of social identity for members of a disadvantaged group. Peer criticism One problem with the foregoing study, however, was that the distraction condition (a car advertisement) did not adequately model the type of questionnaire-based distraction typical in large-scale tests of the status-legitimacy hypothesis. Hence, it is unclear, whether a distraction more consistent with those typically seen in large-scale studies (e.g., the completion of scales measuring other variables unrelated to identity or system justification) would similarly attenuate the salience of gender identity. Replication Study Design The aim of this replication and extension is, for the most part, to address the foregoing criticism. We will expose participants to two conditions designed to either dilute or preserve the identity salience effects of the GSJ scale through task order: Dilution condition: Participants in this condition will complete the GSJ scale first, followed by three scales unrelated to gender identity and system justification, before the word-fragment completion task in the original study. The 3 unrelated scales are: the Exploratory Measure of Multiple Motives (Rubin, 2017), the 10-item Big Five Inventory (Rammstedt & John, 2007), and the Self-Regulatory Focus Scale (Higgins et al., 2011; simplified by Hodis & Hodis, 2016). Undiluted condition: Here, participants will complete the three unrelated scales first, followed by the GSJ scale immediately prior to the word-fragment task. Unlike the original study, this replication focuses exclusively on the GSJ scale completion condition (excluding the national identity scale, and the distractor condition in the original study). Hence, the design will be a 2 (distraction: dilution vs. undiluted) × 2 (identity salience: gender-related vs. gender-unrelated word-fragment completions) mixed design. Distraction is manipulated between-subjects and test the identity-distraction hypothesis. Here the dilution condition models the type of distraction commonly embedded in large-scale surveys. Meanwhile the undiluted condition provides a direct test of the identity-trigger hypothesis. Hence, identity salience is manipulated within-subject in the same way as the original study: participants will be provided word-fragment tasks that can be completed either with gender-related words or words that are unrelated to gender identity. Greater number of gender-related word fragment completions indicates greater salience of gender identity, and we predict that this pattern should be evident in the undiluted condition relative to the diluted condition.

title: Replication of Johns et al
abstract: Word learning is a fundamental process in language development which facilitates vocabulary growth. From mid-childhood, reading becomes the primary source of word learning, where repeated exposure to unfamiliar words enriches a robust mental lexicon (Duff, Tomblin and Catts, 2015). While reading promotes vocabulary expansion through repeated encounters with novel words, the quality of reading experience also determines how effectively these words are integrated into lexical representations that store meaning (Nation, 2017). Johns, Dye, and Jones (2016) explored reading experiences by investigating how contextual diversity influences word learning, recognition, and comprehension. Contextual diversity refers to the variety of linguistic contexts words are encountered in and is argued to significantly influence how a person learns and remembers that word (e.g., Adelman et al., 2006). Johns et al. (2016) tested the effects of contextual diversity on word learning using predictions derived from the Semantic Distinctiveness Model (SDM) (Jones et al., 2012; Johns et al., 2014), which proposes that contextually diverse information increases attention during word encoding and thus enhances memory. More specifically, according to the SDM, words learned in varied contexts develop stronger memory traces because more attention is directed to the unique features associated with each exposure. In Johns et al.’s (2016) experiment, participants read high- and low-variability passages containing a pseudoword. The high-variability condition placed pseudowords in passages with diverse thematic contexts, whereas in the low-variability condition, pseudowords were placed in semantically similar thematic contexts. The results indicated that comprehension of the passages was overall lower in the high-variability condition and increased more over the 5 passages in the low-variability condition. In a surprise pseudo-lexical decision task (PLDT) after completing the passage reading, participants were presented with the trained pseudowords as well as untrained (foil) pseudowords and asked if they recognised the word or not. Pseudowords learned in high-variability conditions were recognised more quickly and accurately than those learned in the low-variability condition. However, in a semantic similarity judgement task, where participants rated the similarity of real-word associates to learned pseudowords, pseudowords learned in low-variability contexts had higher similarity ratings, demonstrating formation of more coherent meaning representations. Johns et al. proposed a trade-off, in which contextually diverse learning supports the development of stronger memory traces, consistent with the SDM, while similar contexts support more coherent semantic understanding. More recent research by Norman et al. (in prep) provides contrasting evidence. Their study also examined the effects of high vs. low diversity learning of pseudowords. Participants learned 8 pseudowords by reading 10 sentences about each. In the low diversity condition, all sentences focused on the same topic whereas in the high diversity condition, they were all on different topics. No effect of diversity was found on an old-new decision post-test (similar to the pseudolexical decision task in Johns et al., 2016). In a word association post-test, where participants generated synonyms for the learned pseudowords, high-variability context learning lead to the generation of a greater proportion of accurate synonyms. These results suggest that learning in high-variability contexts enhances the ability to extract meanings. These conflicting findings highlight uncertainty about whether contextual diversity influences word form learning and whether it strengthens or compromises semantic coherency. Regarding semantic coherency, one possible explanation may relate to differences in how learning was measured (Norman et al., 2025). Johns et al.’s (2016) semantic similarity judgement task tests how well participants can retrieve a specific meaning decided by the experimenter, which might correspond less precisely to the meaning representations extracted for words learned in high- than low-variability contexts. In contrast, Norman et al.’s (in prep) word association task tests participants’ ability to generate their own meaning and learning in high-variability contexts may be beneficial because it provides participants with more information about a word from which to extract a core meaning. To address this, our study will replicate Johns et al. (2016) while incorporating Norman et al.’s (in prep) word association task. This design aims to address whether contextual diversity influences aspects of word learning depending on the task used to assess it. It is predicted that diverse relative to less diverse contextual learning will enhance recognition accuracy and reaction time in the PLDT but reduce accuracy on the semantic similarity judgement task, as in Johns et al. (2016), while also supporting more accurate word association responses, as in Norman et al. (in prep).

title: SPRING ISU RESEARCH METHODS IN PSYCHOLOGY CREP - REPLICATION PROJECT: EMPATHY AVOIDANCE, Ames, Iowa, March 2026
abstract: We are completing this replication as a part of a group project in our research methods in psychology class at Iowa State University. The purpose of this current research is to investigate the reliability, validity, and generalizability of the findings of the study by Cameron and colleagues’ (2019) through a replication. Cameron and colleagues (2019) were interested in whether participants who perceived empathy as cognitively taxing would avoid choosing to behave empathetically without any other extraneous factors present –such as monetary, time, or emotional impacts. The specific aim of this replication study is to investigate a potential association between when a person is presented a choice to avoid empathy and perceived cognitive effort needed to behave empathetically. Empathy is considered a virtue, yet people often avoid empathy. Why is this so? Our undergraduate research methods class (PSYCH 3020) at Iowa State University is conducting a replication project of a published study that offered an answer to this question, organized through the Collaborative Replications and Education Project (CREP). The goal is to teach research methods while simultaneously having students engage in actual research that will be published with data collected from other replication sites. Our class is conducting a replication of the first study that appears in Cameron, Scheffer, Hadjiandreou, Hutcherson, Ferguson, and Inzlict (2019). The class consists of 18 undergraduate students, led by Professor Tess Neal and Graduate Teaching Assistant Maya Irvin-Vitela. The course is designed such that every student is engaged in writing a research paper reporting on our replication project, writing an ethics proposal for Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval, doing a preregistration through the Open Science Framework (OSF), and making an academic poster and presentation based on the project. As a class, we use the jigsaw method to combine work done by individual students into whole single projects (e.g., a single collaboratively written IRB proposal that we actually submit for approval, a single version of a collaboratively-written preregistration that we'll actually submit and use). Our OSF project page, which publicly documents our process, progress, and outcomes, is: https://osf.io/vay9k

title: PSY300 - Levari Replication Study
abstract: This study is intended to be a replication of the “Prevalence-induced concept change in human judgment” study conducted by Levari et al. in 2018. The main question tested in that study was whether people’s definition of a concept expands when that concept becomes less common. In our replication study, that means testing whether participants start recognizing purple dots as “blue” when the number of actual blue dots they see decreases. We predict that the effect observed in the original study will replicate in our sample; that when the prevalence of blue dots decreases over time, participants will start to label more purple dots as “blue”. In other words, when blue dots become rarer, participants' idea of what counts as “blue” will expand. We expect to see this pattern only occur in the decreasing-prevalence condition, and not in the stable-prevalence condition. The control condition would be where the proportion of blue dots remains constant. If we were to successfully replicate this effect, it would suggest that prevalence-induced concept change is reliable across all the different participant samples. Our main dependent variable is the percentage of dots that the participants identify as “blue.” Each dot shown varies along a blue-purple range, and participants decide on each trial whether the dot is blue to them or not. We will measure this by looking at the percentage of dots labeled as blue during the first 200 trials and comparing that to the percentage in the final 200 trials. The change in the proportion of the number of blue dots responds to all conditions. There will be 2 conditions where each participant will be shown a series of colored dots one at a time and decide whether each is blue or not. In the stable-prevalence condition, the number of blue dots stays the same throughout the entire study. In the decreasing-prevalence condition, the proportion of blue dots will gradually decrease after the first 200 trials, while the proportion of purple dots will increase accordingly.

title: Study 16: Replication of Ward et al., 2010 (Cancer Cell)
abstract: Replication of "The common feature of leukemia-associated IDH1 and IDH2 mutations is a neomorphic enzyme activity converting alpha-ketoglutarate to 2-hydroxyglutarate”. title: Replication of ‘Promoting Conservation Behaviors by Leveraging Optimistic and Pessimistic Messages and Emotions’ in a European Context
abstract: This study investigates whether optimistic and pessimistic conservation messages influence emotional responses and conservation-related intentions. The original study by Martell & Rodewald (2024) found a small but significant effect of pessimistic messages on donation intent, but no clear effects on pro-conservation behaviors or political action intentions. We replicate this design in a European context using updated stimuli based on European biodiversity trends. Participants will be randomly assigned to pessimistic, optimistic, combined, or control conditions and will report emotional responses and intentions to donate, engage in conservation behaviors, and participate in political actions. Our goal is to assess whether both the observed and non-observed effects generalize to a European sample.

title: Spontaneous Inferences of Morality and Competence - Replication Study
abstract: The present study examines spontaneous trait inferences (STIs) from morality and competence-related behaviors. Specifically, we will compare the extent to which perceivers make STIs of morality and competence from simple positive and negative behaviors. This will be a conceptual replication of a previous study with new materials.

title: Perceivers’ Categorizations of Multiracial Faces as a Function of Geographic Context: A Pre-Registered Replication of Pauker et al
abstract: This study attempts to replicate the key finding reported in Pauker et al. (2018) that perceivers' ability to categorize multiracial faces as multiracial depends on geographic contexts. In line with the original Pauker et al. (2018) study, participants will be sampled from Hawaii and outside of Hawaii (specifically Southern California) and multiracial categorization data for these two samples will be compared. In addition to this primary test, we will also test three additional hypotheses that were explored by Pauker et al. (2018), though to be clear, we view these tests as secondary to the primary goal of the current replication attempt. First, we will explore whether the composition of the multiracial faces corresponds with differences in categorizations as multiracial, and second, we will test whether racial composition interacts with sample location. Finally, we will test whether contact with multiracial people mediates the relationship between region and multiracial categorizations. In attempting to replicate these focal effects, we will also test for potential differences in hypodescent.

title: Conceptual Replication and Extension of Cohen et al
abstract: The results of Cohen et al. (1991), who discovered that higher psychological stress levels increased susceptibility to the common cold, are conceptually replicated in this work. Participants in the current research will not be exposed to a virus, in contrast to the initial study. Rather, over the course of three weeks, the study will examine the relationship between everyday sickness symptoms and naturally occurring stress in a sample of college students. An expansion of this study looks at sleep quality as a moderator. The objective is to find out if people who have more stress and less sleep exhibit more signs of illness than people who simply have one of these risk factors.

title: Spontaneous construction of causally relevant spatial models: Bulgarian replication of the model-type effect
abstract: When we read narratives such as novels or short stories, we often spontaneously imagine the space the authors are describing. Much psycholinguistic research has focused on the role of these mental situational models that readers create in order to understand sentences or related text. In a series of classic and often cited studies of sentence comprehension, John Bransford and colleagues (Bransford et al., 1972; Johnson et al., 1973) reported that by constructing mental models, participants also made implicit inferences from those models. As a result, participants found it difficult to distinguish sentences they had heard from new sentences if the latter matched the constructed situational model. For example, if participants heard the sentence "Three turtles rested on a floating log, and a fish swam beneath them," they might later falsely recognize that they had heard a sentence finishing with "beneath it" rather than "beneath them". The reason for the misrecognition is that the two sentences stem from the same mental model: (turtles above a log, all above a fish). However, if instead of "on a floating log" the original sentence contained "next to a floating log", participants were much less likely to confuse the original with new sentences, presumably because the two sentences stemmed from two different mental models: (turtles next to a log, the former above a fish) or (turtles next to a log, the latter above a fish). Although this model-type effect is often cited in cognitive psychology and psycholinguistics textbooks, we have been unable to reproduce it in the game demonstrations we have conducted almost every year during psycholinguistics classes. Two previous published replications of Bransford et al.'s (1972) study (Jahn, 2004, Rinck et al., 2001) were but partially successful. Rinck et al. (2001) noted that although the effect was observed, it was much smaller than the original one. In particular, Bransford et al.'s participants (Experiment 1) could not distinguish between old and new sentences stemming from the same model. In contrast, Rinck et al.'s participants did distinguish between old and new sentences; they just did better so when the sentences stemmed from different models than from the same model. Similarly, Jahn's findings did not provide evidence that participants confuse old and new sentences. Accordingly, both replication studies (Jahn, 2004, Rinck et al., 2001) focused on new sentences alone as evidence for the model-type effect. In addition, Jahn (2004) argued that in order to spontaneously construct a mental model, the reader must expect that spatial relations are causally relevant, that is, important for understanding causal relationships, which is the ultimate reader's goal in narratives. For example, if the fish under the three turtles is a shark, the reader will be motivated to create a mental model to represent the relative location of the predator and potential prey. However, if there is a mackerel under the three turtles, readers will be less motivated to construct a mental model because it is not as obviously relevant to understanding causal relationships. In support of his hypothesis, Jahn reported that novel sentences derived from the same spatial model as the old ones were more difficult to identify as new than were novel sentences based on a different model, but only if they referred to predator scenes. Data collection during my in-class game demonstrations had many methodological limitations, most importantly group administration and fixed order of stimuli. The stimuli we used also differed from the stimuli used by Bransford et al., which turned out to be unavailable (Jahn et al., 2004). To address these limitations, in 2022 I designed an online experiment closely following Jahn's (2004, Experiment 1) design and using Jahn's stimulus sentences translated into Bulgarian). Administration was individual and the order of sentences randomized. Unlike Bransford et al. (1972), I found no significant model type (same/different) by probe type (old/new) interaction effect on the recognition scores. Unlike Rinck et al. (2001), the main effect of model type for new sentences was not significant, although it was in the expected direction. Unlike Jahn (2004) there was no significant model type by scene type (predator/peaceful) interaction effect on recognition scores. Due to a bug in the experiment script, some sentence groups occurred more often than others. Now I aim to replicate Bransford et al.'s, Rinck et al.'s, and Jahn's results, with a new improved script and with a new set of participants. The results would thus test the model-type effect in a Bulgarian context, and thus also the theories behind it. There might be reasons why participants do not reliably use spontaneous mental models in this context, although they might do in other contexts. One reason might be that the number of models to construct is just too large to maintain in memory, so participants give up at one point. Given the sentences are quite similar to one another, they might also be subject to interference within the both encoding and retrieval phases.

title: Replication of Barrick et al
abstract: This is a pre-data collection registration of one analysis from Barrick et al. 2024 (Individual differences in emotion prediction and implications for social success) for a Stanford graduate course, Psychology 251 (Experimental Methods), described fully in "Aslarus Replication Report.qmd." All planned analyses and exclusions are reported. The planned sample size is 100 and the rationale and calculations for this sample size are given in the report.

title: Replication of Turri, Buckwalter and Blouw's (2015) study on Justified True Belief
abstract: We are a group of undergraduate student researchers from Masaryk University, Czech Republic. Our aim is to replicate Turri, Buckwalter and Blouw's (2015) study which explores the issue of Justified True Belief (JTB), trying to establish in which situatons and under which circumstances people attribute agent's success to knowledge and when to luck. We carry out this replication study as a part of the Accelerated CREP Project.

abstract: This project holds the materials and raw data for a series of replications of Burgmer & Englich's (2012) finding that manipulating power strongly impacts motor performance. This project now contains the materials and data for 5 separate direct or conceptual replications of Burgmer & Englich (2012). Of these, 2 were pre-registered prior to data collection.

abstract: Pre-registered replication of the core experimental groups from Experiment 3.1 in 10.1016/j.nlm.2023.107858. Reminder + Tetris vs Reminder + Video. Expected replication of the impaired test recall in Reminder + Tetris compared to Reminder + Video.

title: Replication of Ballinger & Crocker (2020) Study 4
abstract: This research project is a direct replication of Study 4 from Ballinger and Crocker's (2020) "Understanding Whites' Perceptions of Multicultural Policies: A (Non)Zero-Sum Framework?", adapted for the United Kingdom context. The original US study challenged prevailing assumptions by demonstrating that White Americans do not necessarily perceive multicultural diversity policies—which explicitly value racial and ethnic differences—as threatening to their identity, contrary to the "exclusion hypothesis" that suggests majority groups feel excluded by such policies. The primary purpose is to test whether this "nonzero-sum" finding generalises to the UK, where different historical contexts, public discourse around multiculturalism, and demographic patterns may influence how White employees perceive diversity policies. This replication is theoretically important because it tests whether the nonzero-sum perception of multiculturalism reflects a broader phenomenon in Western democracies or is specific to the contemporary American context. We will replicate the original 2 (Diversity Policy: colorblind vs. multicultural) × 2 (Status Threat: threat vs. control) factorial design with UK employees (target N = 860). Participants will read about a fictional company's diversity policy and report anticipated social identity threat across four indicators: bias expectations, belonging, negative affect, and performance expectations. Our pre-registered analysis plan includes: (1) direct replication using the original weak priors to enable direct comparison; (2) confirmatory testing with theory-informed directional priors to provide a more rigorous test; and (3) equivalence testing to determine whether any effects are practically meaningful (|d| < 0.20). We will use sequential Bayesian analysis with pre-specified stopping rules (BF₀₁ ≥ 10 or ≤ 0.1) to ensure efficient data collection. Expected outcomes include either: (a) replicating the null effect, suggesting majority groups' nonzero-sum perceptions of multiculturalism generalise across Western contexts; or (b) finding increased identity threat, indicating important cultural moderators. Both outcomes would significantly advance our theoretical understanding of when and why diversity initiatives may or may not trigger majority group backlash, with practical implications for implementing inclusive organisational policies. Preliminary disclosures: - Due to timing constraints, data collection started before the submission of this pre-registration. At present, ~130 responses have been collected but we have not viewed any of them. - Generative AI (Gemini 2.5 and Claude 4 Opus) was used to draft the registration; all details were reviewed and edited by the first author.

title: A replication of Griskevicius et al
abstract: This project is a replication study. We seek to replicate experiment 2 from the following paper: - Griskevicius, V., Tybur, J. M., Delton, A. W., & Robertson, T. E. (2011). The influence of mortality and socioeconomic status on risk and delayed rewards: A life history theory approach. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 100(6), 1015–26.

title: Aesthetic Chills and Political Orientation: A Proposed Replication of Christov-Moore et al
abstract: This project is a proposed registration of Christov-Moore et al.'s 2025 study "Individual differences in aesthetic experience point to the role of bodily awareness in political orientation." In this proposed replication, I suggest the use of electrodermal activity instead of self report as a measure for chills, and a slight change in the stimuli used to elicit chills in participants.

title: Testing the effect of contextual cues on behavioral intentions in the Prisoner’s Dilemma
abstract: We conducted two replications of Kay & Ross (2003) about the effect of cooperation/competition priming on perceptions, beliefs, and decision in a Prisoner's Dilemma game. The first study aimed to replicate the main effect of priming. The second (pre-registered) study intended to replicate the whole 2x2 original study. Before carrying out the replications, we conducted three preliminary studies to adapt the Scrambled sentences task to Argentinean language and culture.

title: Pragmatic and Syntactic Influences on Adjective Interpretation 2.0: A Conceptual Replication of Wittenberg, Barner, and Levy (2016)
abstract: This study employs a 2×2 between-subjects design crossing Sentence Type (command vs. question) with Adjective Order (canonical “tall red” vs. non-canonical “red tall”). Each participant is assigned to one condition and encounters only sentences of that type. On Display 1, participants see a 5×2 grid of 10 objects that vary along a color continuum (the relevant graded dimension) and an additional scalar property (e.g., height). On each trial, they are presented with a sentence from their assigned condition, such as: Canonical command: “Click on the tall red building!” Non-canonical command: “Click on the red tall building!” Canonical question: “Is there a tall red building?” Non-canonical question: “Is there a red tall building?” On Display 2, four new objects of the same type appear: two clear members of a target color, one ambiguous-color object, and one clear non-member. Participants then answer a follow-up question, such as: “How many red buildings would Fiba count here?” They respond by selecting any number of the four objects. This second display assesses whether any threshold adjustment from Display 1 (e.g., treating the ambiguous object as “red”) generalizes to a new array.

title: Cardiac Exercise Risk Study, Replication
abstract: This is a replication of my pre-registered pilot study. For this replication, the changes from the original registration are: Sample: Like the prior sample, participants must be age 60 or older. For this replication, 50 of my participants must have responded yes to any of prolific's coronary artery disease pre-screener options and the other 50 must have responded no. Added Questions: For this study, I added 9 questions to the ambiguous risk scenario section since the pilot. The added questions are as follows: - Based on this doctor's advice what do you think the risk of having a heart attack is if you don't add exercise to your daily routine? (0-100) - Based on this doctor's advice, what do you think the risk of having a heart attack is if you add exercise to your daily routine? (0-100) - Based on this doctor's advice, what do you think the risk is of exercise itself? (0-100) - This doctor is competent (0-7 likert) - I trust this doctor (0-7 likert) - After talking to this doctor, it is clear to me what to do next (0-7) - The doctor should have given me more information on how much exercise is the right amount for me (0-7) - It is impossible for the doctor to know exactly how much exercise is the right amount for me (0-7) - Earlier we asked you "Based on this doctor's advice, what do you think the risk of having a heart attack is if you add exercise to your daily routine?" When we asked you to think about the risk, what did you think about? How did you go about answering that question? (answer in a few brief phrases, bullet points, or sentences) Deleted Questions: To streamline the survey, we deleted 5 of the 13 exact risk scenarios. Participants will no longer see the risk scenarios for the following percents: 0.01, 3, 5, 7, 9 The remainder of the survey remains unchanged from the pre-registered pilot study.

title: Association of musical training with auditory and speech neural coding and perception
abstract: Numerous studies have reported a link between engagement in musical training and enhanced neural processing and perception of sound, ranging from fine-grained pitch discrimination to the perception of speech in noise, with training-related neural changes emerging as early in the auditory pathways as the brainstem or even the cochlea. Such findings suggest a role for experience-dependent plasticity in the early auditory system, which may have meaningful perceptual consequences. However, the generalizability of the musician advantage remains unclear. For example, small-sized samples often represent extreme ends of the musical spectrum; the nature and magnitudes of the musician advantage are sometimes small or inconsistent; and comparisons between studies are complicated by methodological differences and varying analytical techniques. This multi-site study aims to examine the robustness of the musician advantage across the adult lifespan by replicating and extending eight key experiments involving both perception and neural coding across a large sample of listeners.

title: Reassessing Cannabis’ Cognitive Effects in Mice: Replication of Okon et al
abstract: The present study is a conceptual replication and extension of Okon et al. (2015), who examined the effects of long-term Cannabis sativa administration on visuospatial learning in CD1 mice. The original study reported that cannabis-treated mice showed impaired learning and memory in the Morris Water Maze task. As cannabinoid research has advanced significantly over the past decade, there is a need to reassess these conclusions using more rigorous and contemporary research practices. The purpose of this replication is to re-evaluate these effects using a larger and more diverse sample, an expanded set of dose treatments, and three age groups (young, middle-aged, and old) to assess whether THC produces dose and age-dependent changes in cognitive performance. We expect low-dose THC (0.3–1 mg/kg) to preserve or improve cognitive performance, particularly in older mice, while higher doses (10–20 mg/kg) are expected to impair learning across all ages.

title: Direct replication and extension of Mazar and Zhong’s (2010, experiment 3) moral licensing experiment with environmental attitude as moderator of moral regulation processes
abstract: This study aims to conduct direct replication of Mazar and Zhong’s (2010, experiment 3) moral licensing experiment and extend it by including environmental attitude as a moderator of moral regulation processes and by including a control group.

title: Public Perception of Physicians Who Use Artificial Intelligence - An Extended Replication
abstract: This project is an extended replication of Reis et al. (2025), “Public Perception of Physicians Who Use Artificial Intelligence.” The original study examined how patients evaluate physicians who use AI tools in clinical contexts (diagnostic, therapeutic, or administrative). Reis et al. found that physicians who use AI were perceived as less competent, trustworthy, and empathetic, and that participants were less willing to see such physicians, with no significant differences between AI use types. Our extended replication reproduces the original diagnostic AI and control conditions and introduces an additional “diagnostic AI / calibrated” condition. In this new condition, participants receive more specific information about when and how AI is used, emphasizing physician agency, medical competence, and evidence-based application. The project aims to test whether the negative evaluations found in the original study are due to general AI aversion or to insufficiently calibrated communication about AI use.

title: Replication of Exp1 of Corps&Rabagliati(2020)
abstract: This is a pre-data collection registration of replication of Exp 1 of Corps & Rabagliati (2020), described fully in Replication Report Template.qmd. All planned analyses and exclusions are reported. The planned sample size is 80 and the rationale and calculations for this sample size are given in the report.

title: Legal interpretation & coordination -- direct replication of Hannikainen et al
abstract: We conduct a direct replication of the incentivized experiment described by Hannikainen and colleagues (2022). Participants will be presented with 8 vignettes, and for each will decide whether the (over- or under-inclusive) rule has been violated by the actor's behavior. Half of the participants will be asked to provide their personal judgment, while the other half will be incentivized to coordinate their response with a matched anonymous partner, without the possibility of communication. Study materials and protocol match those used in the original study. The only major difference is the employed software (Empirica) and the fact that the partners in the incentivized version are actually matched in real time and have to wait for each other after each trial.

title: The Effect of Red on Gender Categorization of Human Body Silhouettes: A Replication Study
abstract: The present study aims to replicate the findings of Chen, Nakamura, and Watanabe (2023), who demonstrated that the color red biases gender categorization of human body silhouettes. Their study showed that applying red to the body itself increased female categorizations, while applying red to the background decreased female categorizations, resulting in more masculine judgments. The current project searches to find if the effects can be reproduced within a Western cultural context. The experiment examines how color influences gender recognition by manipulating either the color of the body silhouette or the color of the background (red, grey, or green), while also modifying body shape using different hip-to-waist ratios. Participants will be asked to categorize each silhouette as male or female. The study follows the original experimental design, stimuli, and analytical approach to ensure good comparison. The results of this study will contribute to understanding the robustness and cultural generalizability of color-induced biases in social perception.

title: Inducing Awe to Foster Humility: A Replication Study
abstract: This study is a direct replication of study 3 by Stellar, Gordon, Anderson, Piff, McNeil, & Keltnar, 2018. Participation is open to individuals aged 18 and over, and they are being recruited from West Liberty University students and community members via online community groups. Participants (target N ≥ 100) are randomly assigned to an awe inducing condition, involving watching a short video showing the expansion of the universe, or to a neutral control condition, involving watching a nonemotional instructional video about building a wall. Following the induction, participants write about their personal strengths and weaknesses, imagining they are discussing these qualities with a person they just met. Participants failing to follow instructions, such as not listing both strengths and weaknesses, will be excluded from analysis, consistent with the original methodology. It is hypothesized that participants in the awe condition will demonstrate a more balanced view of their strengths and weaknesses to others compared to those in the neutral condition. This is based on the original study hypothesis 2: Momentary experiences of awe increase humility more than neutral or positive comparison states. This replication contributes to the literature on emotion and character strengths by testing the robustness and generalizability of an effect linking awe to humility. The results may have implications for interventions designed to cultivate humility through emotional experiences. Humility is observable across many different cultures and the findings of these studies can help to scientifically capture a construct. Present research provides evidence that having a sense of awe allows individuals to join into social groups more easily by lowering self-interest. Awe may be more strong in collectivist cultures and further study can help to extend those findings to other cultures. Furthermore, this project supports broader efforts toward transparency, reproducibility, and rigor in psychological science, addressing the importance of validating foundational findings across diverse samples.

title: Conceptual replication of unconscious perception findings from emotional Stroop studies
abstract: This study will test the hypothesis that traditional Stroop effects can be obtained with display parameters based upon studies of emotional Stroop effects. The first experiment will be a dissociation design that compares Stroop effects under subliminal and supraliminal conditions. A second experiment will use a single-task, factorial design approach.

title: Assessment of Strength Coaches' Perceptual Accuracy in Identifying Velocity Loss and Repetitions in Reserve Thresholds in the Barbell Squat and Bench Press: A Series Multi-Site Replication Study
abstract: Autoregulation in resistance training adjusts load or volume based on individual performance or perception of performance. While athletes commonly use repetitions in reserve (RIR) and ratings of perceived exertion (RPE) scales, these methods have varying definitions and require experience from the athlete, and fail to account for mechanical changes due to fatigue or load. Although velocity-based training (VBT) effectively monitors daily performance variations, its cost and impracticality limit its usefulness. Recent research suggests coaches can assess athlete performance through perception of velocity loss (PVL) by measuring changes between the first and subsequent repetitions or perception of repetitions in reserve (PRIR) by predicting an athlete's remaining repetition capacity. These methods could provide cost-effective alternatives to VBT while standardizing training intensity assessment and enhancing coach-athlete communication. Therefore, this study aims to compare coaches' PVL and PRIR assessments against direct measurements of VL and RIR at 60% and 80% 1RM in the barbell squat, bench press, and deadlift. We hypothesize that coaches will demonstrate greater accuracy in assessing PVL thresholds in comparison to PRIR thresholds across all exercises and intensities. This research study will be a repeated measures crossover design replicated across five study sites. A total of 120 coaches (24 per site) will each evaluate 24 videos of a trainee performing SQ, BP, and DL at 60% and 80% 1RM. Coaches will identify the repetition at which the trainee in the video exceeds target thresholds for both PVL and PRIR conditions, using high and low anchors in proximity to failure. A negative binomial generalized linear mixed effects regression model will be used to examine absolute errors between variables: condition (PVL or PRIR), threshold in proximity to failure (low or high anchor), load (60% or 80%1RM), exercise (SQ, BP, or DL), and order. The outcomes of this study will determine the superior model (PVL or PRIR) for a coach to implement. Results from each research site (N = 5) will be incorporated into a random effects model to account for between-site heterogeneity. Data will be pooled and analyzed in aggregate. This comprehensive analysis will provide a complete picture of coaches’ assessment abilities across all participating institutions (Springfield College, University of the West of Scotland, Tel Aviv University, eCampus University Italy, and University of Rome “Foro Italico”). Understanding how accurately coaches perceive VL and RIR thresholds would enable more precise adjustments to training programs, leading to optimized performance and reduced injury risk. Consequently, our multi-site approach strengthens this investigation by providing findings that can be generalized across diverse strength and conditioning settings.

title: Belief Superiority Preregistered Replication
abstract: There is currently a debate in political psychology about whether dogmatism and belief superiority are symmetric or asymmetric across the ideological spectrum. One study found that dogmatism was higher amongst conservatives than liberals, but both conservatives and liberals with extreme attitudes reported higher perceived belief superiority (Toner, Leary, Asher & Jongman-Sereno, 2013). Our goal was to conduct a pre-registered direct and conceptual replication of this previous research using a larger and more nationally representative sample. Consistent with prior research, we found that conservatives had higher dogmatism scores than liberals while both conservatives and liberals with extreme attitudes were associated with higher belief superiority compared to those with more moderate attitudes. Moreover, whether conservative or liberal attitudes were associated with higher belief superiority was topic dependent. Different from prior research, we found that ideologically extreme individuals had higher dogmatism. We discuss the implications of these results for theoretical debates in political psychology.

title: Talking About the Silence – Identifying the Language of Ostracism
abstract: In a first study with a German sample, we found that linguistic style differs when participants wrote about social exclusion vs. social inclusion. To back up those results, we aim to replicate them in a different language (English) and with a different sample. We also test additional hypotheses emerging from exploratory analysis conducted in our first study.

title: A Replication and Extension of “Getting what you expect: How civil servant stereotypes affect citizen satisfaction and perceived performance.” OSF Registries
abstract: This study replicates and extends Bertram et al.’s (2024) “Getting what you expect: How civil servant stereotypes affect citizen satisfaction and perceived performance” in the context of public service delivery in China. The original study shows that the activation of negative stereotypes leading to lower levels of satisfaction and perceived performance. Building on that design, we implement a 3 (stereotype activation: negative vs. positive vs. control) × 3 (public service context: regulation oriented vs. service oriented vs. both regulation and service oriented) between-subjects vignette experiment in China. Beyond this, we distinguish between experimentally activated stereotypes and individuals’ internalized stereotypes about civil servants, and test how their interplay affects subsequent perceptions and evaluations of public services. Specifically, we address three research questions: (1) Does the activation of stereotypes about civil servants shape citizens’ perceived performance and satisfaction with public services? (2) Do the activation of stereotypes and individuals’ internalized stereotypes interact in shaping perceived performance and satisfaction? (3) Are the effects of stereotypes on perceived performance and satisfaction heterogeneous across different types of public services? By providing a cross-cultural replication in a non-Western administrative context, this study clarifies how stereotypes operate as predictive expectations in citizens’ experiences of public service delivery, and contributes to broader debates on the classic Expectancy–Disconfirmation Model in citizen satisfaction research.

title: Replication of Anchoring Effect with Cognitive Load as Boundary Condition
abstract: Literature Review: The anchor effect, described by Tversky and Kahneman (1974), is a strong cognitive bias where numerical predictions are oriented toward previously presented high or low numerical anchors. Various experimental research paradigms (e.g., random number wheels, reference values ​​given in questions) have demonstrated the consistency of this effect. Furthermore, the strength of the anchor effect may depend on the decision-maker's cognitive load intensity; for example, under high cognitive load, individuals may adhere more to intuitive methods. Literature Gap: While the scope of the anchor effect is well-documented in the literature, studies on whether cognitive load strengthens the anchor effect are lacking. This study aims to address this gap by replicating the classical anchor paradigm while introducing cognitive load as an additional boundary condition to test the interaction domain. Present Study: This study will utilize a full factorial design between subjects of 2 (Anchor: High vs. Low) × 2 (Cognitive Load: High vs. Low). Participants will first be asked a reference question (e.g., "Is the percentage of UN member states in Africa greater than or less than the reference value?"), followed by numerical estimates. Cognitive load manipulation will be performed by asking participants to memorize numbers during the task (High load: 7-digit number; Low load: 2-digit number).

title: Direct Replication of a Research Claim from Wurst et al (2017), From Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
abstract: This is a Direct Replication attempt on the Claim 4 claim The results of the correlation and regression analyses are shown in Table 7: Participants higher on Rivalry were less satisfied with their relationships. title: Replication of Muenks et al., 2020
abstract: This is a pre-data collection registration of a class project that is replicating study 1 of Muenks et al. (2020) paper published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: General. This replication is described fully in "preregistration.Rmd." file found in the "pilot" folder, or on Rpub: https://rpubs.com/ramyalol99/1375440 All planned analyses and exclusions are reported. The planned sample size is 129 and the rationale and calculations for this sample size are given in the report.

title: Study 5 — Replication of Latent Profiles of the Experience of Ambivalent Classism Inventory (EACI) in a Sample of Women and Men Experiencing Homelessness.
abstract: Once the EACI profiles among economically disadvantaged women and men have been identified, we will examine their existence and replicability in a sample of people experiencing homelessness. Given the particularities associated with extreme social exclusion, different patterns from those found in the previous study may emerge — for instance, a higher prevalence of profiles characterised by hostile experiences. Similarly, both the predictors and the consequences associated with these profiles may differ from those observed previously. As in the preceding study, we will conduct a latent profile analysis (LPA) using a convenience sample of people experiencing homelessness (SINHOGAR survey) to examine how these profiles are configured and distributed at the individual level. We will explore the existence of distinct profiles based on participants’ subjective experiences with ambivalent classism, distinguishing between those who experience high or low levels of hostile classism and/or benevolence.

title: Does Closeness Foster Leniency? How Psychological Distance Shapes Moral Judgments
abstract: The present bachelor's thesis is a replication of the third study by Eyal, Liberman and Trope (2008) and examines how psychological distance influences the judgment of immoral behavior. More specifically, it analyzes whether low social distance leads to more lenient evaluations than high social distance when assessing the behavior. The planned study is based on Construal Level Theory (Trope & Liberman, 2010), which conceptualizes how the mental representation of an object or event changes depending on psychological distance. Social distance is one of the four widely discussed dimension of psychological distance (temporal, spatial, social and hypothetical), capturing the sense of closeness to the self and one's own experience (Lo et al., 2019; Soderberg et al., 2015). For example, the self is the closest point on the continuum of social distance, followed by close others like family members and friends, then acquaintances, whereas strangers are perceived as more socially distant. When social distance is low, a low construal level is activated, under which concrete features and situational details of a target object are considered (Trope & Liberman, 2010). However, when distance is high, a high level of construal dominates and abstract characteristics or superordinate principles are taken into account (Zang et al., 2022). Construal level influences judgments in moral contexts (Eyal & Liberman, 2012; Zhang et al., 2022). Therefore, it is expected that immoral behavior will be judged harsher when judged from another person's perspective than one's own. This is due to the consideration of abstract moral principles under a high construal level when social distance is high. In contrast, judgments from one's own perspective under a low construal level should be more lenient (Eyal et al., 2008). Those expected results align with the findings in the original study. As an extension to the original study, judging immoral behavior from a stranger's perspective should create even higher social distance and lead to an even harsher judgment compared to the perspective of a specific person.

title: Replication of Gervais and Norenzayan (2012) - Analytic Thinking Promotes Religious Disbelief
abstract: The goal of this project is to conduct a high-powered multi-site direct replication of the finding by Gervais & Norenzayan that analytic thinking is correlated with and causes diminished religious belief.

title: Exp 3: Features to trait path replication
abstract: This is a pre-registered replication of prior studies we conducted. The study examines whether women higher in performed femininity are judged as less likely to be a scientist than women lower in performed femininity. It also examines whether performed femininity affects perceptions about being a scientist over and above categorization as a woman.

title: Replication of Gable & Harmon-Jones (2008, Psych Science, 19(5))
abstract: This is an independent replication of a study, originally conducted by Gable & Harmon-Jones (2008) showing that positive affect high in approach motivation reduces the breadth of attention (i.e., more local than global focus).The replication will include an exact replication of Experiment 2 described in the original paper, comparing positive affect high in approach motivation with neutral affect, as well as a conceptual replication, using culturally adapted affective stimuli and comparing positive affect high in approach motivation, positive affect low in approach motivation and neutral affect within one experiment.

title: Replication Experiment: The Effects of Task Difficulty and Internal States on Time Perception
abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this experiment is to determine the effects of task difficulty, task duration, and people's appraisals of task features on their perception of time. Research Question: Which elements of a task influence the perception of time passing? Objective: This study will consider how task difficulty and task duration interact with time estimation. This study will also pose new research questions that aim to explore the relation between certain task qualities and individual factors and time perception. We will replicate a task that was conducted in our lab by using a visual and memory search task programmed on an online platform (Qualtrics) so that participants can do the experiment from home. Therefore, participants in the present experiment will all know that they are supposed to keep track of time, but will not be using time-keeping devices to do so. As such, this experiment aims to investigate intentional time-keeping. This will help us better understand how well people estimate the time when they purposefully keep track of it. This will refine our understanding of fundamental processes underlying the intentional perception of time. Contemporary cognitive models in this area of research make specific predictions regarding the effects of task difficulty and task duration, yet the tasks used to investigate these effects differ greatly from one experiment to the next. For example, past experiments have employed a range of activities including a Stroop task (Zakay & Fallach, 1984; Predebon, 1999), memorizing and rehearsing lists of items (Miller, Hicks, & Willette, 1978), listening to a piece of music (Brown & Stubbs, 1988; 1992), and even watching a boiling pot of water (Block, George, & Reed, 1980). There is a need to replicate the task used across experiments to rule out extraneous variables that may be specific to each task. By using the same task (visual and memory search) across multiple experiments, conclusions can be made from the data with increased confidence. This present experiment will also examine what features of a task (e.g., perceived difficulty, engagement, etc.) and what internal experiences common throughout the task (e.g., fatigue, distractedness, mind wandering, mindfulness, etc,) impact time perception (exploratory analyses). This will help lay the groundwork for future experiments investigating how external and internal factors might influence time perception.

title: <i>Amendment to existing registration: Replication of a Research Claim from Vollmann et al
abstract: This registration is an amendment to the inferential criteria of the previously registered Replication of a Research Claim from Vollmann et al. (2011), from The European Journal of Personality (available at https://osf.io/afw29; currently under embargo until March 8, 2024 unless made public earlier).

title: Direct replication of “Temporary suppression of visual processing in RSVP task: an attentional blink?” (Experiment 2)
abstract: This project aims at a direct replication of RAymond et al. (JEP:HPP, 1992) “Temporary suppression of visual processing in RSVP task: an attentional blink?” (Experiment 2) with a much larger number of participants (N=100 in contrast to the N=10 of the original paper).

abstract: Replication of "Discovery and Preclinical Validation of Drug Indications Using Compendia of Public Gene Expression Data”. Includes information to prepare the replication experiments. Includes data, code, and digital materials from completed replication experiments.

abstract: In this resource, you can find the Dataset, R code script and Supplemental Materials related to the article “Stereotype Threat Effects on Italian Girls’ Mathematics Performance: A Failure to Replicate”.

title: Replication of Sex and Syntax/Boroditsky 2003
abstract: I hope I can change this description later on because it's 1 in the night and I'm going to bed now. Anyways, this is going to be the pre-registration for an attempt to replicate, as close as I can, an experiment of Lera Boroditsky; specifically, the "missing study" from Boroditsky 2002, Sex, Syntax and Semantics, where Spanish and German native speakers were reported to have given grammatical gender-congruent descriptions to words that differ in grammatical gender between German and Spanish. For example, Germans were reported to have described "Die Brücke" as fragile and pretty, Spaniards described "El puente" as sturdy and tall.
