title: How does an eyewitness’ type of confidence (numeric versus verbal) and level of confidence statement affect mock jurors’ judgments of the accused and their interpretation of confidence? A replication
abstract: The experiment will look at how an eyewitness’s type of confidence statement and level of confidence affect mock jurors’ judgements of the accused and their interpretation of the confidence level. It is a replication of our first experiment, using a broader range of vignettes.

title: Study 44: Replication of Berger et al., 2012 (Nature)
abstract: Replication of "Melanoma genome sequencing reveals frequent PREX2 mutations”. Includes information to prepare the replication experiments. Includes data, code, and digital materials from completed replication experiments.

title: An Online Replication of the Misattribution of Fatigue
abstract: Exactly what it says on the tin: This project is aimed at replicating with online methods the results of our laboratory study on the misattribution of fatigue. The design is fundamentally the same as our previous laboratory study, but the specific procedures are adapted for online data collection.

title: Replication of Dyreng et al
abstract: This project aims to replicate the main tables and figures in Dyreng, Hanlon, Maydew, and Thornock (2017, JFE) on corporate effective tax rates over 1988–2012, using Compustat data and their published sample and variable definitions.

title: Preregistered Replication of Study 5 from "Exploring the Socioeconomic Pattern of Humans’ Future Orientation"
abstract: Purpose: This study investigates how perceived socioeconomic status (SES) influences individuals’ future orientation (FO). The aim is to provide a preregistered, well-powered replication of a previously observed effect. Design and Manipulation: Participants will be undergraduate Psychology students completing an online survey in individual cubicles. Subjective SES will be measured using the MacArthur scale (Adler et al., 2000), and participants will be randomly assigned to either a low-SES or a middle-SES condition, controlling for their subjective SES. The manipulation uses a simulated society called Bimboola (Jetten et al., 2015), where participants choose items such as houses, vehicles, phones, and leisure activities appropriate to their assigned SES group. Choices for the low-SES group are intentionally less attractive to strengthen the manipulation, and participants’ perception of their group’s wealth and income will be assessed to verify the effectiveness of the manipulation. Procedure and Expected Results: Future orientation will be measured both before and after the SES manipulation. Filler tasks unrelated to the study’s main objectives will separate the pre- and post-measures to reduce potential bias. The session will be completed in a single sitting, and participants will receive a full debriefing. Based on previous findings, we expect that low-SES manipulation will increase focus on immediate consequences and fatalism, while reducing optimism.

title: Check Their Head: Implications of the Scarcity and Replicability of Manipulation Checks from the Reproducibility Project
abstract: Our analysis will focus only on the significance of the MC test as different from zero in the direction of the original study (analysis 4b from the Supplementary Materials of the Science article). This is because we are interested in what the significance of the MC in the replication study might say about the conditions of that study specifically, rather than what it might say about the existence of the effect overall. We will produce a table, excluding original effects and manipulation checks that were reported as nonsignificant (although numbers of these categories will be reported, they are expected to be small). The table will cross a) whether the key effect was judged to be successfully replicated by analysis 4b, with b) whether the MC was judged to be a successful replication of the original MC by the same criterion.

title: Replication of Smiley & Fisher (2022)
abstract: This is a replication of Smiley and Fisher's (2022) Experiment 1, in which participants are presented with an unfamiliar technology and randomly assigned to believe that the technology was invented 15 years before or after their birth. This is a test of the status quo bias as a psychological mechanism explaining skepticism toward technologies.

title: Independent Cross-Temporal Replication of Coalition Phase Transition in Cognitive Resource Allocation: A Preregistered Validation Study
abstract: This preregistration specifies confirmatory hypotheses and a complete analysis plan for Study 2, an independent- sample replication of findings from Study 1. BACKGROUND AND RATIONALE Study 1 (completed prior to this preregistration) was a cross-sectional exploratory study (N = 1,457) examining how five cognitive-affective variables — Learning Belief Strength (LBS), Self-Monitoring Capacity (SMC), Perceived Survival Concern (PSC, operationalized via public self- consciousness), Brief Fear of Negative Evaluation (BFNE), and Attentional Control Scale (ACS) — interact to predict dual-channel adaptive outcomes: Learning Adaptation (G_Adapt) and Social Adaptation (S_Adapt) among Chinese university students. Study 1 employed a multi-method analytic framework including EBICglasso network analysis, information- geometric diagnostics (Total Correlation, O-information), segmented threshold regression, Transformer-based deep learning with SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) decomposition, and hypergraph-based coalition strength analysis. Study 1 data collection, analysis, and manuscript preparation were fully completed before this preregistration. STUDY 1 KEY FINDINGS (basis for all predictions): (a) Phase transition in the Learning channel: Segmented regression identified a statistically significant threshold at LBS γ = 4.18 [95% CI: 3.80, 6.00] (Davies test p = .0055, ΔAIC = −11.28). The LBS → G_Adapt slope approximately doubled from β₁ = 0.122 (SE = 0.021) below the threshold to β₂ = 0.228 (SE = 0.014) above it, representing a shift from medium (β* = 0.31) to large (β* = 0.58) standardized effect. No significant threshold was detected in the Social channel (S_Adapt ~ LBS; Davies p = .386). (b) SHAP sign-flip of the Growth Coalition: Transformer- derived SHAP analysis revealed that the Growth Coalition (LBS + SMC) contribution to Learning Adaptation reverses sign across LBS regimes: suppressive (mean SHAP = −0.238) in the Survival- dominant regime (LBS < 3.75) and facilitative (mean SHAP = +0.223) in the Growth-dominant regime (LBS ≥ 4.75). This sign-flip was replicated across 20 independent random seeds (100% sign consistency), with regime membership accounting for 42% of SHAP variance (η² = .420, F(2, 1454) = 526.44, p < .001). (c) Channel asymmetry: Learning Adaptation showed 2.83× larger regime sensitivity than Social Adaptation (η² = .167 vs. .059; F ratio = 145.44 vs. 45.41). (d) Coalition coherence U-shape: System-wide coalition coherence (5-Way metric) exhibited a U-shaped trajectory across LBS intervals — high coherence at LBS extremes (0.961 at LBS < 2.81; 0.757 at LBS > 5.23) and fragmentation during the transition zone (0.554 at LBS 4.02–4.63). (e) Prediction–Explanation Dissociation: The optimized Transformer achieved slightly lower global predictive accuracy than linear models (R² = .280 vs. .309) but revealed qualitatively richer process information (the sign-flip) invisible to constant-coefficient models. STUDY 2 PURPOSE Study 2 collects an independent sample (target N = 500) from the same institutional population approximately one month after Study 1, using identical measures. Its primary purpose is to test whether the four core findings above replicate in a new sample at a different time point. All hypotheses below are derived exclusively from Study 1 results and are registered before any Study 2 data are collected or inspected. PROSPECTIVE DESIGN NOTE Study 2 also collects the last four digits of each participant's student ID number. This identifier is not used in any Study 2 analysis but is collected prospectively to enable individual-level longitudinal linkage should a future Study 3 (within-person follow-up) be conducted. The decision to conduct Study 3 will depend on peer review feedback; this contingency is documented transparently.

title: Study 12: Replication of Johannessen et al., 2010 (Nature)
abstract: Replication of "COT drives resistance to RAF inhibition through MAP kinase pathway reactivation”. Includes information to prepare the replication experiments. Includes data, code, and digital materials from partially completed replication experiments.

title: Replication Study: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) use in Preventing Compliance with Command Hallucinations
abstract: The study is a direct replication of the 2014 Lancet Psychiatry study, “Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) use in Preventing Compliance with Command Hallucinations,” with an additional demographic extension. It analyzes the potential use of Cognitive behavioral therapy in the treatment of command hallucinations. More specifically, the reduction in perceived voice power results in resistance to compliance.

title: A Replication Study on the association between Birth Order, Attachment Style and Jealousy
abstract: This research project aims to replicate the original study "Birth Order and Romantic Relationship Styles and Attitudes in College Students" by Emily M. McGuirk & Terry F. Pettijohn II. It is a dissertation project for Northumbria University BSc Psychology with Criminology. See ethics document for further information.

title: “Judgments of cause and blame: The effects of intention and blame”: A pre-registered replication of Experiment 2 in Lagnado and Channon (2008)
abstract: In this manuscript we replicated experiment 2 as found in Judgment of Cause and Blame: The effects of intention and blame from Lagnado and Channon (2008). Moreover we upload all data, stimuli, analysis scripts, survey templates as well as links to a pre-registration and document pre-print history in an effort to increase transparency and reproducibility of the experiment.

title: Incentives Bending Truths: A Conceptual Replication Of Deception Dynamics
abstract: This is a conceptual replication and extension of Rong & Houser (2016). Understanding group deception dynamics while adding a new condition to understand the complexities of deception behavior within real-world environments.

title: Study 5: Replication of Ricci-Vitiani et al., 2010 (Nature)
abstract: Replication of "Tumour vascularization via endothelial differentiation of glioblastoma stem-like cells”. Includes information to prepare the replication experiments. Includes data, code, and digital materials from partially completed replication experiments.

title: Replication of the stroop effect with bilingual vs monolingual status as a boundary condition
abstract: The Stroop effect is one of the most robust findings in cognitive psychology. In the classic Stroop task, people are slower to name the ink color of a word when the word’s meaning conflicts with the ink color (e.g., the word “green” printed in red). This interference demonstrates how automatic processes, such as reading, compete with controlled processes, such as selectively attending to color. Because of its reliability, the Stroop effect is widely used as a benchmark for testing theories of attention, conflict monitoring, and cognitive control. A major line of research has examined whether individual differences influence the magnitude of the Stroop effect. One widely discussed factor is bilingualism. Bilingual individuals constantly manage two active language systems and often must inhibit the non-target language. Some researchers argue that this continuous practice strengthens executive control abilities, including inhibition and conflict resolution. If this is true, bilinguals might show reduced interference in tasks like the Stroop, because they are more efficient at suppressing irrelevant information. Early studies (e.g., Bialystok et al., 2004) supported this idea and reported that bilinguals outperform monolinguals on several executive function tasks. However, more recent research has questioned the reliability and generality of the “bilingual advantage.” Some studies find no difference between bilinguals and monolinguals, while others report that advantages only appear under certain conditions, such as high task difficulty or specific age ranges. Meta-analyses also suggest that the effect may be smaller than originally proposed. These inconsistencies create a gap in the literature: we still lack simple, transparent replications specifically testing bilingualism as a boundary condition of classic cognitive effects like the Stroop. This preregistered study aims to address this gap by replicating the Stroop effect and testing whether the size of the interference differs between bilingual and monolingual participants. By doing so, it evaluates whether bilingualism moderates performance in a highly standardized measure of cognitive control. This is theoretically important because it helps clarify whether bilingual language experience translates into general cognitive advantages, and under what conditions such advantages might appear. Gap in the literature: Although many studies explore bilingualism and executive function, fewer focus on the Stroop task in particular, and even fewer report fully transparent preregistered replications. Additionally, much of the classic research was conducted in controlled laboratory settings. With the increasing use of online testing platforms, it is valuable to examine whether previously observed patterns replicate in more naturalistic online environments. This study directly targets these gaps by offering a preregistered, online replication with a clear individual-difference moderator. Present study: The present study aims to replicate the classic Stroop effect and examine whether bilingual vs. monolingual status serves as a boundary condition. Specifically, the study will test whether bilingual individuals show reduced interference (smaller congruent–incongruent reaction time difference) compared to monolingual individuals. This preregistered design aims to increase transparency and contribute to the ongoing debate about the bilingual advantage in cognitive control.

title: Replication of Stellar, Gordon, Anderson, Piff, McNeil, & Keltner (2018; Study 3) at Northern Arizona University
abstract: As a part of the Collaboration Replication and Education Project (CREP), we are replicating Stellar et al. due each of us having an interest in this study as well as wanting to dive deeper into the findings the original researchers have found. This study tested whether or not inducing awe increases humility. Stellar et al. hypothesized that awe leads to greater humility through an enhanced appreciation of others. The nature of the replication is to provide more confirming information on the effectiveness of Study 3 of Stellar through a different participant pool in a college environment. The target sample size for this project is 120-125 which will be recruited through SONA and will be conducted through an online survey.

title: Beliefs that Empower: Educators’ Background-Specific Strengths Beliefs enhance Motivation and Academic Outcomes among Lower-SES Students – A partial Replication and Extension in Germany
abstract: This study aims to replicate and extend the experimental study “Educators’ Beliefs About Students’ Backgrounds as a Pathway for Supporting Motivation” by Silverman et al. (2023), by testing the generalizability of its findings in a German university context. We will investigate whether exposure to messages of educators with background-specific strengths (BSS) beliefs, compared to a control condition, increases students' own BSS beliefs, their identity-based motivation (IBM, Oyserman & Destin, 2010) outcomes, academic persistence, and performance, particularly among students from lower socioeconomic status (SES) backgrounds, and whether these effects are mediated by students’ own BSS beliefs.

title: Replication of Social Intuition: Behavioral and Neurobiological Considerations
abstract: This is a replication of Jellema et al. (2024), "Social Intuition: Behavioral and Neurobiological Considerations." This is a social implicit learning paradigm that investigates participants' abilities to learn the disposition of an actor towards them. This study will recruit neurotypical adult participants on Prolific. While the participants will be neurotypical, the study includes the Autism Quotient-10 to probe autistic traits. In the acquisition phase of this paradigm, the happy face condition will start with gaze forward, smiling and gradually shift to gaze away from the participant, frowning. The angry condition will start with gaze forward, frowning and gradually shift to gaze away from the participant, smiling. In the test phase, a combined face of 60% maximally smiling agent A and 40% maximally smiling agent B will progress in steps of 5% towards 60% maximally smiling agent B. Participants will see this four times. Then the same thing will be repeated for the frowning faces, and the participants will see this four times as well. At the end, participants will be asked questions probing whether they detected the contingencies in the experiment and if they did their data will be excluded. This study expects to find that participants will judge the composite face in the happy condition to be most like agent A (happy disposition) and the composite face in the angry condition to be most like agent B (angry disposition).

title: PSYCH 251 Replication of Study 2 by van Prooijen et al
abstract: This research aims to replicate a key experimental finding in the literature on illusory pattern perception - the tendency to perceive structure, meaning, or intentionality in randomness. Prior work suggests that individuals differ in the extent to which they detect patterns where none exist, and that this perceptual bias may contribute to the formation and endorsement of irrational beliefs, including conspiracy theories, supernatural beliefs, and susceptibility to misinformation. However, the empirical evidence linking pattern perception to such beliefs has been mixed, highlighting the need for well-powered and transparent replication efforts. This study focuses on Study 2 from van Prooijen et al. (2018), one of the few experiments that directly manipulates reliance on intuitive pattern search rather than indirectly inducing pattern perception through uncertainty, lack of control, or existential threat. In the original study, participants viewed random sequences of coin tosses and were instructed either to rely on intuitive, pattern-seeking reasoning or to engage in more analytic, deliberative processing. Participants encouraged to rely on intuition perceived more structure in randomness and subsequently reported stronger irrational beliefs. Because this paradigm isolates the pattern-perception mechanism itself, it provides a strong empirical test of whether intuitive processing causally increases perceived patterns and irrational belief endorsement. The current project will replicate this paradigm in an online setting using Qualtrics for survey implementation and Prolific for participant recruitment. Participants will be randomly assigned to one of two instruction conditions (intuitive vs. analytic), will evaluate a series of random coin-toss sequences, and will complete measures of conspiracy and supernatural beliefs. This replication will examine both the experimental main effect (intuition increases pattern perception) and the associational component (greater pattern perception predicts stronger irrational beliefs).

title: Replication and Extension of Stephens, Hamedani, and Destin
abstract: Part of my dissertation research will be a replication and extension of Stephens, N. M., Hamedani, M. G., & Destin, M. (2014). Closing the social-class achievement gap: A difference-education intervention improves first-generation students’ academic performance and all students’ college transition. Psychological Science, 25, 943-953. The entire committee-approved dissertation proposal (2015_04_27_dissertation_proposal_Clark.pdf) is included, but only Parts I and III are relevant to this registered replication and extension (refer to this document for background and hypotheses). Explicit description of what will be directly replicated and what will constitute extension is included as a separate document in the project descriptions folder (replication_and extension.docx). A third document in the project descriptions folder (analysis_plan) reiterates and elaborates on analysis plan information contained in the proposal. The fourth document in the project descriptions folder is an update about logistical and administrative challenges that will affect wave 0 (i.e., baseline) surveying, but will ultimately not affect analysis replication. Materials to be used in the intervention itself (e.g., scripts) are further developed from the original proposal and are included in the project materials folder. Materials to be used in surveys (i.e., measurements) are also included in the project materials folder. The committee-approved proposal contains known typos that suggest more than one intervention will be conducted. The proposal prior to defense was to implement Stephens and colleagues' (2014) difference-education intervention and Walton and Cohen's (2011) social-belonging intervention for side-by-side comparison. Upon defense, my committee recommended focusing on and maximizing sample size for the difference-education intervention. Only the difference-education intervention will be implemented, and if the target sample size (n=450) is reached, it will be triple the size of the sample in the original study.

title: Replication of Superficial Auditory (Dis)fluency Biases Higher-Level Social Judgment by Walter-Terrill, Ongchoco & Scholl (2025, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences)
abstract: This is a pre-data collection registration of a replication of Walter-Terrill, et al. (2025, PNAS), described fully in "replication_report.qmd." All planned analyses and exclusions are reported. The planned sample size is 250 and the rationale and calculations for this sample size are given in the report.

title: Smurfing: Judgments and Blame [Student Sample Replication]
abstract: This preregistration represents a direct replication attempt of a prior study on smurfing in video games. In this study, we simply seek to assess whether the findings of Smurfing: Judgments and Blame will generalize and replicate to a convenience sample of undergraduate students. In other words, many concerns about student samples have been raised in recent years, specifically as it pertains to if effects found in student samples are generalizable to broader/actual populations of interest. We consider this question to be empirical. Therefore, we are directly and exactly replicating all procedures and methods in our second study (wherein we recruited our sample from small gaming forums on Reddit) in a convenience sample of undergraduate students at a large midwestern university. For convenience, we have copied the exact registration language from our initial preregistration of Smurfing: Judgements and Blame below, and highlight here that the only differences in this preregistration may be found in the data collection procedures section of the sampling plan.

title: Behavioral Synchrony and Cognitive Performance: Replication and Possible Mechanisms
abstract: This project aims to replicate a small study that found that when people engaged in behavioral synchrony, they showed improved word recall and face memory compared to people who did not engage in behavioral synchrony (Macrae et al., 2008). We will begin by attempting to replicate Macrae and colleagues' (2008) findings. If this replication is successful, we will introduce an additional condition to examine the mechanism by which Macrae and colleagues’ (2008) manipulation was successful.

title: Investigating Fast Mapping (FM) in healthy adults using an implicit memory measure: An additional condition (FM-r) for our replication study
abstract: To investigate potential mechanisms claimed to support fast mapping in adults, we will add an FM-r learning condition to the previously pre-registered design. FM-r is identical to the FM condition, but it does not include the simultaneous presentation of a known referent picture beside the unknown item whose name is to-be-incidentally-learned. I pre-registered a replication proposal https://osf.io/6kmnf/ in March 2019 for an online study that aims to replicate and extend one of our previous Fast Mapping (FM) results. I am now pre-registering an additional learning condition to that protocol. The pre-registration of this additional condition, to be run in a between-participant design, is being made prior to data collection for any of the conditions, including those previously pre-registered.

title: The conspiracy beliefs trap: longitudinal replication of Adam-Troian et al
abstract: Results of the project are now published in Adamus et al. (2026). Longitudinal analysis shows possible distinct patterns of associations between conspiracy beliefs and either institutional distrust or the sense of precarity. British Journal of Social Psychology, 65(1). https://doi.org/10.1111/bjso.70036

title: Regional differences in the experience of awe and replication of associations between awe facets, psychedelic experiences, and mental-health outcomes. OSF Registries
abstract: This project investigates the structure, correlates, and regional variability of the experience of awe, with a particular focus on awe occurring in the context of psychedelic experiences. Awe has been increasingly recognized as a complex, multi-faceted emotional state associated with perceived vastness and the need for cognitive accommodation, and it has been linked to a wide range of psychological and well-being outcomes. However, the structure of awe, its relationship to other altered states of consciousness, and its expression across regions remain understudied. The present study has two primary aims. First, it seeks to examine the convergent and divergent validity of a 12-item short form of the Awe-Experience Scale (AWE-SF) in a large, global sample of individuals reporting on psychedelic experience. This will allow for further validation of a brief, multi-faceted measure of awe suitable for use in large surveys, clinical research, and cross-cultural contexts. The study will examine how the AWE-SF relates to personality traits, mental health, and persisting effects outcomes to confirm whether previously reported patterns replicate in a diverse global sample. Second, the project will examine regional similarities and differences in the structure and expression of awe. Participants will be recruited from multiple countries and cultural backgrounds. This will help determine whether the six-facet structure of awe—Vastness, Accommodation, Self-loss, Connectedness, Altered Sense of Time, and Physiological Responses—operates similarly across regions, and whether the intensity or profile of awe experiences differs between them.

title: Replication of Bainbridge, Hall, Baker 2019, Nature Communications
abstract: Bainbridge et al. (2019) uses a free recall drawing paradigm to investigate the diagnosticity of visual memory for static, real-world scenes. Their results show that participants’ drawings, both immediately and after a delay, could reliably capture object and spatial information. The study is methodologically rigorous, incorporating drawing, memory, and rating tasks. While replicating the free drawing component is too resource-intensive, we recruit new participants on Prolific to complete the drawing-to-picture matching task using the existing drawing dataset, allowing for an assessment of the robustness of the original main effect.

title: Registered Report for Replication of Sussman and Olivola (2011)
abstract: Direct replication and extension of: Sussman, A. B., & Olivola, C. Y. (2011). Axe the tax: Taxes are disliked more than equivalent costs. Journal of Marketing Research, 48, 91–101. http://doi.org/10.1509/jmkr.48.SPL.S91 The following pre-registrations were filed for this project: Pre-registration of in-principal accepted stage 1 report: osf.io/7pruq Pre-registration for analyses requested by reviewers: osf.io/nqg3e Pre-registration for pre-tests: osf.io/g2jbr

title: Replication of the effect of a sweet taste on prosocial behavior
abstract: In line with recent research in embodied cognition, Meier, Moeller, Riemer-Peltz and Robinson (study 5; 2012) found that experiencing a sweet taste causes an increase in prosocial behavior. This project aims to closely replicate their fifth study.

title: Motivational priming and positive affect during exercise: A replication study
abstract: This study aims to replicate findings of Pottratz et al. (in press) with a larger and more diverse sample of participants. Pottratz et al. (in press) showed that watching music videos with affective primes (positive valenced words) during a workout leads to significantly higher in-task affective valence, post-exercise enjoyment, remembered pleasure and forecasted pleasure compared to watching the same music videos without primes. In contrast to the original study, data analysis in the replication study will be performed with hierarchical multi-level regression analysis, in order to account for the nested data structure.

title: The Effect of Red on Gender Categorization of Human Body Silhouettes: A Replication Study
abstract: The present study aims to replicate the findings of Chen, Nakamura, and Watanabe (2023), who demonstrated that the color red biases gender categorization of human body silhouettes. Their study showed that applying red to the body itself increased female categorizations, while applying red to the background decreased female categorizations, resulting in more masculine judgments. The current project searches to find if the effects can be reproduced within a Western cultural context. The experiment examines how color influences gender recognition by manipulating either the color of the body silhouette or the color of the background (red, grey, or green), while also modifying body shape using different hip-to-waist ratios. Participants will be asked to categorize each silhouette as male or female. The study follows the original experimental design, stimuli, and analytical approach to ensure good comparison. The results of this study will contribute to understanding the robustness and cultural generalizability of color-induced biases in social perception.

title: Replication of Kuehn et al., 2012
abstract: In this study we aim to replicate one of the key findings from the paper by Kuehn et al. (2012, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jad.2012.03.024) “Why ruminators won´t stop: The structural and resting state correlates of rumination and its relation to depression”. This replication is part of the overarching project “Replication of Findings in Neuroimaging – MDD” (ReFiNe-MDD, https://osf.io/n86q9/) using data from various cohorts. The project aims to a) estimate the percentage of replicable findings in brain structural gray matter correlates related to variables relevant for depression, b) identify study characteristics associated with replicability of neuroimaging findings, and c) deduct methodological guidelines to foster replicability of findings in this area of research. Therefore, a minimum of 60 single replications will be conducted. In this single replication, we will focus on the association of gray matter volume and rumination in healthy controls. Kuehn et al. (2012) found rumination to be negatively associated with clusters in bilateral inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), bilateral anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and bilateral mid cingulate cortex (MCC) in healthy individuals. Additionally, we will examine whether this association can also be found in depressed patients.

title: The Drivers of Willingness-to-fight in Europe: a European-wide Replication of a Belgian Large Sample Study
abstract: In a context of renewed tension and increasing defence budget in Europe and around the globe, being able to understand what drives people (un)willingness to defend their country in case of war is especially timely. To do so, two main theoretical frameworks are tested in a complementary way to account for such costly behavioural intentions: attitudes and identity. First, in line with the cognitive consistency literature, different attitudes linked to peace and war, as well as foreign policy, are tested as potential drivers of the willingness to fight in case of a war (WtF). Second, the importance of the individual's identity in relationship to their country and with Europe is tested. On the one hand, identification and fusion with one's country and Europe are tested as complementary drivers of WtF. Those two concepts linking the personal and collective level of identity are said to drive WtF, but in different ways: identification increases the level of external threat perceived, which drives the WtF, whereas fusion increases the trust in group's members which leads to higher level of readiness to commit costly pro-group behaviours, including WtF. On the other hand, on top of the level of identification with a group, the qualitative nature of this identity can also drive different level of WtF. To do so, the concepts of patriotism, nationalism and democratic patriotism are tested as potential drivers of the WTF for one country (nationalism/patriotism) and for the EU (democratic patriotism).

title: <i>The Effect of Uncontrollable vs
abstract: Executive functions (EF) are as set of higher-order, goal directed mental processes that enable individuals to focus, inhibitate, regulate their behaviour and manage complex tasks, particularly in situations where automatic responses are not enough (Diamond, 2012, p.136). Miyake et al. (2000) propose that there are three core EFs, working memory, inhibitory control and the flexible shifting of attention and that these abilities are essential for performing goal-oriented behavior by integrating various streams of information. Also, these cognitive processes are dependent on prefrontal cortex, making them particularly vulnerable to disruption by phsiological and psychological states such as acute stress. However, as emphasized in a recent review by Plieger and Reuter (2020), emprical finding on stress and executive functioning remain complex, some studies report impairments, while others suggest improvements, largely depending on moderating variables such as task complexity and the type of the stressor. The authors argue that stress may not simply reduce cognitive capacity but may instead make the brain rely more on automatic responses to preserve energy under stress A meta analysis by Shields et al. (2016) supports the sensivity of EFs, though the effect are not uniform across all domains. They demonstrated that acute stress significantly impairs core executive fuctions, espacially working memory and cognitive flexibilty. The impact on inhibition is less straightforward and showed more nuanced pattern. While stress tends to impair cognitive inhibition, it may sometimes enhance response inhibition. Consistent with the impairment view, Starcke et al. (2016) used the Paced Auditory Serial Addition Test (PASAT-C) to induce acute stress and found that stressed participants performed significantly worse than the non-stressed participants on the Color-Word Interference Test (stroop), meaning that uncontrollable stress distort the ability to filter interference. However, the impairment observed by Starcke et al. (2016) might not be due to stress intensity alone, but rather the uncontrollable nature of the stressor (unavoidable aversive noise). Henderson et al. (2012) investigated this distinction and found that controllability is a key moderater. In their study, participants exposed to uncontrollable stress showed no relationship between stress and performance whereas those who learned to control the stressor showed reduced Stroop interference, meaning that realizing that they had control over the stressor improved their performance. This suggests that the perception of control buffers individuals against the effects of stress on executive funtions. In other words, when individuals percieve that they have some degree of control over a stressful stimulus, their cognitive functions are less disrupted. Furthermore, in line with the Hendorson et al. (2012), Gathmann et al. (2014) showed that in certain high-demand conditions, brain uses adaptive mechanisms to preserve performance. This adaptive mechanisms allow individuals to maintain acurracy in stressful situations. In this context, the impairment observed by Starcke et al. (2016) may be caused by the lack of perceived control in their stress manipulation. The primary motivation for this study is to resolve inconsistencies regarding the impact of acute stress on executive functions. While starcke et al. (2016) provided evidence that acute stress impairs inhibition, they used PASAT-C stress induction paradigm which is strictly uncontrollable stressor, leaving it unclear whether the observed impairment was driven by phsiological intensity of stress or the psychological state of helplesness. As highlightened by Plieger and Reuter (2020), identifying moderating factors such as controlability is essential when we try to understand the relationship between stress and executive functions. A clearer understanding of this relationship would lead to a better understanding of cognitive resilience. Therefore, this study aims to replicate the inhibitory impairment reported by Starcke et al (2016) while introducing “perceived controllability” as a manipulated boundary condition. To directly address the original study’s concern that the length of test battery may reduce the stress response over time, the current study will focus only on the Attention and Inhibition component (Stroop Test), administered immediately after the stress induction. By comparing an Uncontrollable Stress group, a Controllable Stress group and a Control group, present study aims to show distorting impact of acute stress on inhibitory performance is reduced when individuals believe they have some degree of control over the stressor.

title: Can Asymmetric Attention to Opportunity Costs effect explain impatience in intertemporal choice？A replication study
abstract: In â€œThe value of nothing: asymmetric attention to opportunity costs drives intertemporal decision makingâ€ Read, Olivola and Hardisty (2017) proposed an asymmetric subjective opportunity cost (ASOC) effect to explain and predict why impatience can be detected in intertemporal choice. This work deserves to be replicated and extended for its novel and potentially important findings. The present study aimed to examine the reliability and robustness of the evidence presented by Read et al. by conducting precise replications of their key findings in Study 1. The ASOC effect (Read, et al., 2017) was important for expanding its application and reported to be typically stronger when baseline larger-but-later option (LL) and smaller-but-sooner option (SS) preferences were closer to 50% in the authorsâ€™ original condition. Therefore, the present study also aimed to replicate and test the ASOC effect when baseline LL preferences were higher or lower than those in the original condition. We intended to set two additional conditions wherein either LL or SS is more obviously favored (i.e., baseline LL preferences were higher or lower than those in the original condition) by respectively applying the common difference effect (Kirby and Herrnstein, 1995) and the unit effect (Burson, Larrick and Lynch Jr., 2009; Pandelaere, Briers and Lembregts, 2011). Having successfully generated two more obviously favored conditions, the ASOC effect was replicated and confirmed under the original condition and one additional condition wherein SS was more obviously favored. However, the ASOC effect was not detected under the other additional condition wherein LL was more obviously favored. The implications of these findings were discussed.

title: Replication of the Stroop Effect with Cognitive Load as a Boundary Condition
abstract: This study aims to replicate the classic Stroop effect (Stroop, 1935) and examine whether cognitive load moderates attentional interference during a color-naming task. Participants will complete congruent and incongruent Stroop trials under low and high cognitive load conditions. It is predicted that reaction times will be slower and accuracy lower in incongruent trials, with greater Stroop interference under high cognitive load. The study will clarify how working memory resources influence attentional control, contributing to cognitive psychology research on executive functions. Keywords: Stroop Effect, Cognitive Load, Attention, Executive Function, Replication

title: Replication of Wu et al., 2021
abstract: In this study we aim to replicate one of the key findings from the paper by Wu et al. (2021). This replication is part of the overarching project “Replication of Findings in Neuroimaging – MDD” (ReFiNe-MDD, https://osf.io/n86q9/, Goltermann & Altegoer, 2024) using data from various cohorts. The project aims to a) estimate the percentage of replicable findings in the area of brain structural gray matter correlates related to variables relevant for depression, b) identify study characteristics associated with replicability of neuroimaging findings, and c) deduct methodological guidelines to foster replicability of findings in this area of research. Therefore, a minimum of 60 single replications will be conducted. In this single replication, we will focus on the interaction effect of perceived stress and age (adolescents vs. middle-aged adults) on gray matter volume (GMV). Wu et al. found associations between perceived stress and the structural volume in multiple clusters across the brain. They found a positive relationship between the levels of perceived stress and the GMV of the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), the insula, and the amygdala in adolescents, whereas these regions were found to be negatively related with perceived stress in adults. Additional to the replication, in a smaller subsample we aim to examine the association of intolerance of uncertainty and GMV, potentially moderated by the level of perceived stress. As the association of perceived stress and GMV has been shown to be inverse in younger vs. middle aged adults, we also assume an inverse association of intolerance of uncertainty and GMV.

title: The Preference for Simple Explanations and Interventions in the Pursuit of Efficiency: Study 1 and 2 – A pre-registered replication of Sehl et al
abstract: People often find information presented in bullet points easier to understand than lengthy prose, and in general prefer simpler explanations over more complex ones. This preference aligns with the principle of Occam’s razor, which holds that unnecessary assumptions should not be introduced, and has been regarded as one of the “explanatory virtues” used to evaluate the quality of explanations. Some have argued that simple explanations are more likely to be true than complex ones. However, it has also been suggested that probability alone cannot fully account for this phenomenon (Vrantsidis & Lombrozo, 2022). Sehl et al. (2024) propose a novel theory that the preference for simplicity is not unique to explanation itself, but rather stems from a broader tendency to favor efficient means of achieving goals. Providing an explanation is a goal-directed activity aimed at understanding the causes of an outcome, and from this perspective, explanations with fewer causes and assumptions can be seen as more efficient. According to this “doing things efficiently” account, the preference for simpler causes should manifest not only when judging why an outcome occurred (explanatory judgments), but also when evaluating how an outcome could be achieved (process judgments). Moreover, the theory predicts that when statistical information about the reliability or generality of causes (e.g., base rates or likelihood of effect occurrence) is provided, the preference for simplicity may weaken or even reverse. Sehl et al. support these predictions with evidence from seven preregistered experiments. However, participants in prior studies were recruited primarily from the United States (via CloudResearch and Prolific), leaving open questions about the universality of these findings. The present study attempts to replicate Experiments 1, 2, and 7 of Sehl et al. (2024), focusing on the claim that preferences for simpler explanations result from the pursuit of efficiency. By conducting this replication with Japanese participants, we aim to test the cross-cultural generality of the findings, broaden the scope of the theory’s applicability, and contribute to comparative research on potential cultural differences in cognitive processes. In this study, we will try to replicate Sehl et al. (2024)’s Study 1 and 2.

title: Replication of Rubin et al
abstract: This project is a replication of Study 1A from Rubin et al.'s paper "Comparing the value of perceived human versus AI-generated empathy" in Nature Human Behavior. The goal of this study is to understand whether the perceived source of a response (i.e., human or AI-generated) affect how empathic participants perceive the response to be. In this between-subjects study, participants will be asked to describe a recent emotional situation and are then told that the generated response is from either another human or an AI response. In both cases, the response is generated by a large language model. Participants are then asked to rate perceived empathy of positive resonance. Following Rubin et al.'s work, we expect that participants will perceive human-generated responses as more empathic compare to AI-generated responses.

title: <i>Replication and Extension of "Detection and Perceptions of Labeled vs
abstract: This preregistration is for a replication of a study which explored the detection of labeled and unlabeled AI-generated images in political social media posts, and spill-over effects on perceptions of the source and on evaluations of accompanying text. This project further extends the original study by considering probative value of the images as a moderating variable, which may change how people react to posts featuring (un)labeled AI-generated images vs. photographs. Moreover, this study is conducted among a larger and quota-based sample, enabling a better generalization of findings.

title: Do Reading Goals Make a Difference for Refutation Text Effectiveness? A conceptual replication of Asberger et al
abstract: There are many misconceptions about educational topics. For instance, it is a widespread assumption that differences in hemispheric dominance (left brain, right brain), originally and scientifically referring to task-related specialization in the brain, can explain individual differences between learners. To overcome such misconceptions, refutation texts appear to be a promising approach. However, it is yet an open question, which factors influence the effectiveness of refutation texts. One factor that possibly influences the effectiveness of refutation interventions may be individuals’ reading goals. A recent study (Asberger et al., 2024, https://doi.org/10.1080/00220973.2024.2358480) showed mixed results regarding the influence of reading goals on conceptual change. We will follow up on their study to further investigate whether different reading goals (reading for an explanation vs. for entertainment) moderate potential effects of a refutation text to elicit conceptual change within preservice teachers about an educational neuromyth (i.e. hemispheric dominance). Specifically, we study in which way text type (refutation vs. traditional text), reading goal (for an explanation vs. for entertainment) and time (before vs. after reading the respective text type) interact and affect beliefs in the hemispheric dominance neuromyth and their confidence-accuracy. The primary change compared to Asberger et al. (2024) concerns the operationalization of the reading goal instructions.

title: The Replication and Extension of Descriptive Gender Stereotypes
abstract: This study aims to cross-culturally examine and expand upon existing findings regarding gender-related stereotypes of thinking styles (namely, that women are more concrete and men are more abstract) and their impact on task assignments. The original study, conducted in the United States, indicated that such stereotypes lead to women being disproportionately assigned to detail-oriented tasks, regardless of the task’s attractiveness. Against the backdrop of China’s collectivist culture, this research investigates the stability of this pattern in the Chinese context and further explores the moderating role of cultural orientation (individualism vs. collectivism). Using a between-subjects experimental design, participants will be randomly assigned to one of three stereotype activation conditions (“women are more concrete,” “men are more concrete,” or control). They will then be presented with a managerial scenario requiring them to assign a task described as either high or low in attractiveness. The task involves selecting one of four fictional employees who vary by gender but are otherwise comparable in qualifications and experience. We anticipate replicating the core finding that women are more likely to be assigned concrete tasks when gender stereotypes are activated. Furthermore, we expect collectivist values to strengthen this bias. The results will contribute to cross-cultural social psychology by testing the generalizability of stereotype-based task allocation mechanisms and will offer practical insights for promoting gender equity in organizational practices within China.

title: Replication of Responsibility Attribution in AI-Advised Decisions
abstract: This study conducts a systematic replication of Passlack et al. (2024), examining how advisor type (AI vs. human) and outcome valence (positive vs. negative) affect self-attribution of responsibility in individual decision-making.

title: <i>Replication: Effect of AI vs
abstract: This study is a pre‑registered replication of an earlier pilot experiment (N = 62) that examined whether attributing ethically questionable advice to an AI system versus a human expert influences moral decision‑making, trust in advice, and ethics perception among young adults in India. The original study found no statistically significant differences between the AI and human advice conditions on any outcome, but it was severely underpowered to detect small‑to‑medium effects (φ ≥ .36 at 80% power). The present replication aims to address these limitations by using a larger, adequately powered sample, validated measures, and balanced group assignment. Primary research questions: (1) Does advice source (AI vs. human) affect the likelihood of making an unethical choice? (2) Does advice source affect trust in the advice? (3) Does trust predict unethical choice?

title: Replication of Muenks et al (2020) at University of Minnesota
abstract: A CREP replication of Study 1 from Muenks et al (2020) "Does my professor think my ability can change? Students' perceptions of their STEM professors' mindset beliefs predict their psychology vulnerability, engagement, and performance in class"

title: Experiment 3: Does participants’ associative memory differ by event components? A replication of Experiment 1 with a between-subjects design and larger sample size. OSF Registries
abstract: This experiment investigates participants' associative memory when reading sentences describing simple causal events. It is a replication of Experiment 1, preregistering a new analysis plan (compared to Experiment 1) and recruiting a larger sample size for increased statistical power.

title: Replication of Friederichs, Jostmann, Kuhl, and Baumann (2022) with shorter audio
abstract: In many situations, "getting things done" poses a real challenge. Even the best intentions are often not translated into action. According to the theory of Personality Systems Interactions (PSI), intention enactment requires the collaboration of two cognitive systems that are antagonistically related and activated by opposing affective states: "Intention memory" (specialized in the representation of intentions, analytical problem-solving, and planning) is activated by low positive affect, whereas "intuitive behavior control" (specialized in executing preprogrammed action steps) is activated by high positive affect. Shifting between high and low positive affect creates a short time window in which both systems are equally activated and able to exchange information effectively so that intentions can be smoothly translated into action. The work by Friederichs and colleagues (2022) shows that systematically training affective shifting increases intention enactment - especially among people with low self-regulatory abilities (i.e., state-oriented rather than action-oriented individuals). Participants practiced affective shifting through 10-minute audios on seven consecutive days. The affective shifting exercise was compared to an affective boosting exercise with audios that stimulated purely positive affect and to neutral control audios. Consistent with expectations, affective shifting increased intention enactment as measured by reduced Stroop interference after intention-forming primes. In the present study, we want to replicate and extend the findings by Friederichs and colleagues (2022). First, we want to replicate findings with a shortened intervention: Does a single 10-minute affective shifting exercise suffice to increase intention enactment in the Stroop task compared to affective boosting and neutral control conditions? Second, we want to extend findings to different outcome variables: Does the affective shifting exercise stimulate spontaneous affective shifting and self-positivity in state-oriented participants when reflecting on a personal intention?

title: Replication of the Misinformation Effect with Source Credibility as a Boundary Condition
abstract: This preregistered study explores the misinformation effect, a well-established memory distortion phenomenon in which exposure to misleading post-event information alters an individual’s recollection of an originally witnessed event. Decades of studies, including classic work by Loftus and colleagues, reveal that people can confidently recall details that were never present when false or suggestive information is presented after the fact. The effect reinforces the reconstructive quality of human memory and is of particular applied importance in legal contexts, where eyewitness testimony may be corrupted through misleading questioning or reports. In accordance with the assignment requirement to replicate an earlier psychological finding, the objective of this study was to recreate the classical misinformation effect via comparing memory accuracy and false-memory endorsement between subjects given false and true information after the event. Successful replication of this mechanism will illustrate its robustness in current sample and experimental conditions. In addition to replicating the original study, this study adds a boundary condition for whether source credibility serves as a moderator of susceptibility to misinformation. While the misinformation effect is well known, less is known about which features of the source of the information be it their expertise or trustworthiness dictate how large memory distortion is. That hypothesis that misleading information from a high-credibility source produces larger misinformation effects than misleading information from a low-credibility source is tested in the study. This test of moderation helps us understand when and why individual participants are at higher risk of memory distortion, with relevance for eyewitness reliability and the study of social influence on memory more generally.

title: The Influence of Minority Status on In-Group Liking from a Power Relations Perspective: A Replication Study with Chinese Sample
abstract: This study constitutes a systematic conceptual replication and extension of Study 4 from “Being in the Minority Boosts In-Group Love: Explanations and Boundary Conditions.” The original research, based on Western individualist samples, proposed that minority status enhances in-group liking through increased perceived distinctiveness, belongingness, and expected cooperation. However, the cultural generalizability, ecological validity, and the role of intergroup power dynamics in real-world contexts remain underexplored. To address these gaps, the present study is conducted within a Chinese collectivist cultural context with the following objectives: first, to examine whether the “minority-boosts-in-group-love” effect persists in a collectivist setting and to identify its cultural boundaries; second, to introduce “power relations” as a central moderating variable, simulating real-world scenarios where minority groups may hold higher, equal, or lower power, thereby investigating how power structures shape group identification dynamics; third, to enhance experimental realism and reduce demand characteristics through methodological improvements, such as embedding a film-viewing task and masked measures. The research employs a 2 (group size: minority vs. majority) × 2 (target: in-group vs. out-group) × 3 (power relations: minority higher, equal, lower) mixed design. A diverse sample will be recruited across multiple regions in China, and variables including in-group liking, distinctiveness, belongingness, and expected cooperation will be measured to analyze the pathways through which power influences group identification. Anticipated outcomes include: first, a potentially attenuated original effect in the Chinese sample, supporting the cultural moderation hypothesis; second, a significant moderating role of power relations, wherein higher minority power weakens the enhancement of in-group liking, whereas lower power strengthens it; third, mediation analyses are expected to reveal that belongingness and expected cooperation play more prominent roles under low-power conditions, while distinctiveness may remain relatively salient under high-power conditions. This study not only provides cross-cultural validation and a power-based extension of Optimal Distinctiveness Theory but also offers evidence-based implications for organizational management, team integration, and intergroup policy design.

title: Replication of Idiosyncratic tower of Babel: Individual differences in word-meaning representation increase as word abstractness increases
abstract: This research project replicates the behavioral task from Wang, X., & Bi, Y. (2021), "Idiosyncratic tower of Babel: Individual differences in word-meaning representation increase as word abstractness increases," Psychological Science, 32(10), 1617-1635. The study has two primary aims: (1) to gain hands-on experience with semantic network methodology, and (2) to investigate individual differences in semantic representation across levels of word abstractness. We hypothesize that we will replicate the original findings, specifically that individual differences in word-meaning representations will be minimal for concrete words but will increase systematically as word abstractness increases. This pattern would support the notion that abstract concepts are represented more idiosyncratically across individuals compared to concrete concepts, which tend to be grounded in more universally shared sensory-motor experiences.

title: Replication of The Radical Flank: Curse or Blessing of a Social Movement? by Dasch et al
abstract: I plan to replicate Dasch et al. (2024)'s study of the radical flank effect--the influence of activists with more extreme ideologies and tactics on a movement. I aim to specifically replicate their first survey experiment, which found that radical flanks increase support for moderate groups.

title: Replication of Tentori, Cruppi, & Russo (2013) at the University of Grenoble-Alpes (CREP #21-36)
abstract: This is a replication of Tentori, Crupi and Russo (2013) about "the Determinants of the Conjunction Fallacy: Probability Versus Inductive Confirmation". Conjunction fallacy is a classic statistical error that describes irrational behavior. This replication will attempt to explain it and reproduce the work of Tentori and al.

title: Replication of "Influence of articulatory suppression on observationally acquired SR binding and retrieval effects"
abstract: This study is a replication of “Influence of articulatory suppression on observationally acquired SR binding and retrieval effects” with the only difference that data will be collected in the lab instead of online.

title: Engagement with fat talk as a function of social comparison and body image concerns: Two replication studies support main effects but do not support an interaction effect
abstract: This project contains the details of two pre-registered replication studies of Corning, A. F., & Gondoli, D. M. (2012). Who is most likely to fat talk? A social comparison perspective. Body Image, 9(4), 528–531. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bodyim.2012.05.004 The analyses underpinning the paper are under 'Analyses'

title: Replication of Granhag et al
abstract: This project aim to replicate Granhag et al. (2013). The goal is to evaluate the effectiveness of the S.U.E. (Strategic Use of Evidence) technique in investigative interviews for discriminating between truthful and fabricated accounts. A quasi-experimental design will be implemented with university students, who will be required to either report or simulate an action and will subsequently be interviewed under one of three possible conditions: early disclosure of evidence, basic S.U.E., and incremental S.U.E. Inconsistencies in the accounts—both in relation to the evidence and within the narrative/statement itself—will be analyzed as a means of assessing the effectiveness of this technique in evaluating credibility.

title: Function Words and their Relationship with Academic Success: A Replication and Extension of Pennebaker et al
abstract: The goal of this study is to replicate and extend Pennebaker et al.’s (2014) study that found that the categorical-dynamic language index measured from undergraduate admissions essays predicted undergraduate grade point averages (GPA). To extend the study, we will also examine CDI’s criterion relationships with first year academic retention, student graduation, and with demographic characteristics including race and sex, both in terms of group mean differences and predictive bias. Additionally, we will examine how agentic language, communal language, lexical diversity, and readability in admissions essays relate to academic success.

title: Independent Preregistered Replication Test of Universal Handedness Preference (Δp_LR ≈ 0.04) Across Quantum-to-Cosmological Scales
abstract: This project hosts the pre-registered protocol for an independent replication test of a reported uniform handedness preference (Δp_LR ≈ 0.04) across diverse physical phenomena and scales. The original analysis (Abshier and Grok, 2026) documented 78 anomalies, classifying 73 as primary probes with consistent directional handedness bias, yielding an effective n ≈ 49 after granular overlap correction and a binomial probability under the 50/50 null of ≈ 1.78 × 10⁻¹⁵. This collaboration with Claude (Sonnet-4) conducts a blind, independent test using a new set of 75–100 peer-reviewed phenomena selected independently of the original swarm entries. The goal is to determine whether the directional handedness preference replicates robustly or reveals important boundaries/refinements. All protocol, selection reasoning, analysis code, decision logs, and results (confirmatory, falsifying, or inconclusive) will be publicly documented and available in the linked GitHub repository. OSF DOI (to be assigned upon public registration) GitHub mirror: https://github.com/tlabshier/CPP-600-Cell-Swarm-Analyses/tree/main/trials/independent-trial-1 This is a collaborative effort to rigorously evaluate the uniformity of handedness across scales through transparent, pre-registered methodology.

title: Does Global Slowing Explain Age Effects in Inhibitory Control? Replication
abstract: A long-standing debate in the study of cognitive aging concerns whether aging results in a selective deficit in inhibitory control beyond a general slowing of cognitive processing. Previous studies have obtained mixed findings, in part because the typical free response time paradigm lacks the specificity required to disentangle component processes underlying inhibitory control. We have recently applied a novel forced-response paradigm and a computational model to disentangle these processes to test if aging results in overall speed differences or a selective deficit in inhibitory control. 50 older adults and 57 younger adults completed a “forced-response” arrow flanker task. We found strong evidence that older adults demonstrate a global slowing of processing, without any selective deficit in inhibitory control. This preregistration is aimed at running a direct replication study of this result. We will again aim to collect usable data from 50 older adults and 50 younger adults, with the same participant and trial-level exclusions. Participants will complete the same forced-response arrow flanker task. Our primary analysis will focus on applying the same computational model of response preparation. We hypothesize that our results from the first study will replicate, where older adults show a slowing of both habitual and goal-directed response preparation, suggesting a global slowing in response preparation rather than a specific deficit in inhibitory control.

title: Study 47: Replication of Lu et al., 2012
abstract: Replication of "IDH mutation impairs histone demethylation and results in a block to cell differentiation". Includes information to prepare the replication experiments. Includes data, code, and digital materials from partially completed replication experiments.

title: <i>A Conceptual Replication and Extension of Newland et al
abstract: Mental toughness plays a major role in sports, and many athletes and coaches treat it as essential for successful performance. Researchers define mental toughness in different ways, which creates challenges for accurate measurement. Some definitions focus on confidence and emotional control, while others describe resilience and persistence. A recent review found that mental toughness tends to support better performance, but the strength of this effect depends on how researchers define and measure it (Cowden, 2017). Because basketball emphasizes psychological resilience and high-pressure decision making, I want to study mental toughness using stronger methods than earlier research. Newland et al. (2013) examined how mental toughness predicted basketball performance. They used the Psychological Performance Inventory Alternative (PPIA) and calculated performance with the PERF score. They also tested gender and starting status as moderators. They found that mental toughness predicted performance only for male starters. They also found that men scored higher on mental toughness than women. These findings raised questions about measurement quality and fairness. The PPIA has unclear structure and limited theoretical grounding, and the PERF score does not consider playing time, which affects how athletes accumulate statistics. I want to replicate this study because these limitations reduce confidence in the original findings. Researchers have noted that older mental toughness scales such as the PPIA do not match modern theories and often fail to measure mental toughness consistently (Crum, 2022). Hughes (2019) describes this as part of psychology’s measurement crisis, where weak tools lead to weak conclusions. A conceptual replication that uses stronger measurement can address this problem. I also want to improve the performance metric because the original PERF score did not adjust for minutes played. Adjusting each statistic by minutes creates a more accurate indicator of true performance. Generalizability is another concern. The original sample included only college athletes from a narrow set of schools. Ghai et al. (2025) explain that psychology often makes broad claims based on limited samples, which they call MASKing. To address this problem, I plan to recruit high school and college athletes and intentionally include Native American and Polynesian athletes. This helps create a more inclusive understanding of mental toughness that reflects different competitive and cultural backgrounds. To improve measurement quality, I plan to replace the PPIA with the Sports Mental Toughness Questionnaire (SMTQ). The SMTQ measures confidence, constancy, and control and shows stronger reliability and clearer structure (Sheard et al., 2009). Research shows that newer mental toughness tools predict performance and emotional stability more consistently than older measures (Cowden, 2017). New findings challenge assumptions about gender differences as well. Kumari and Chauhan (2025) found that female student athletes sometimes score higher on mental toughness than males when researchers use valid tools. This suggests that gender patterns may change when researchers use stronger measures. I also plan to extend the study by including sleep quality as a predictor. Sleep influences recovery, reaction time, focus, and mood. Coel et al. (2022) found that adolescent athletes often experience poor sleep, which affects performance. Silva et al. (2021) found that improving sleep often enhances accuracy and speed. To include sleep in my study, I will use a short version of the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. My sample will include 200 high school athletes and 200 college athletes. I will also include Native American and Polynesian athletes to improve diversity. Banks et al. (2019) emphasize the importance of preregistration and transparency. I will preregister my hypotheses, measures, and analyses to follow these guidelines. Based on this research, I expect the conceptual replication to show a stronger relationship between mental toughness and performance than the original study. I expect this because the SMTQ is a better measure and because adjusting performance by minutes played will reduce error. I also expect sleep quality to strengthen the effect of mental toughness and predict performance on its own. Finally, I expect the SMTQ to work well for both men and women. If it does not, this study will help identify whether sport psychology needs more inclusive tools. Hypothesis 1: I expect my conceptual replication to show a stronger mental toughness and performance relationship than the original study because of the improved measurement tools and adjusted performance metric. Hypothesis 2: I expect mental toughness and sleep quality to predict basketball performance together, and I expect this combined effect to be stronger than the effect of mental toughness alone.

title: A Replication and Extension of findings from McGuirk, E & Pettijohn T, 2008 study on Birth order and romantic relationship styles and attitudes
abstract: A Northumbria University BSc Psychology dissertation. A replication study based on the findings of McGuirk, E., & Pettijohn, T. (2008) on Birth order and romantic relationship styles and attitudes. Looking into whether the findings still hold up in today's day and age.

title: The Replication and Extension of Descriptive Gender Stereotypes
abstract: This study aims to cross-culturally examine and expand upon existing findings regarding gender-related stereotypes of thinking styles (namely, that women are more concrete and men are more abstract) and their impact on task assignments.
